Report_ID: MENQoL sexual subscore (absolute change from baseline to week 12; bother scale, higher = worse sexual function)
Title: Micro-dose transdermal estradiol for relief of hot flushes in postmenopausal Asian women: a randomized controlled trial
Author: Haines C, Yu SL, Hiemeyer F, Schaefers M
Comment: Change-from-baseline scores (mean ± SD of change) used for both arms; no end-of-treatment absolute values reported. MENQoL is a bother scale (higher = worse), so means must be sign-reversed before computing the SMD so that higher = better sexual function. No between-group p-value or test statistic was reported for the sexual subscore. '±' assumed to be SD, consistent with Table 1 footnote ('mean + standard deviation'). M_diff computed as group_2_mean − group_1_mean (placebo − estradiol) = 0.2 on the paper's original (un-reversed) bother orientation.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Transdermal micro-dose 17β-estradiol 0.014 mg/day patch (one patch/week, 12 weeks)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Design Type: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter, parallel-group trial
Country: Thailand, Philippines, Singapore, Hong Kong, Malaysia
Participant type: Symptomatic postmenopausal Asian women aged 40–65 years with at least 24 hot flushes within a 7-day screening period
Recruitment source: Multicenter clinical sites in Thailand, the Philippines, Singapore, Hong Kong and Malaysia
Outcome measurement: Mean ± standard deviation of the absolute change from baseline in the MENQoL sexual subscore at week 12, full analysis set
Outcome variable: MENQoL sexual subscore (absolute change from baseline to week 12; bother scale, higher = worse sexual function)
effect_direction: favours estrogen (after sign reversal of bother-oriented MENQoL: estradiol improved more than placebo; not statistically significant)

Report_ID: Sexual function (MENQOL sexual-urinary problems domain, change from baseline; higher = worse)
Title: Comparison between vaginal royal jelly and vaginal estrogen effects on quality of life and vaginal atrophy in postmenopausal women: a clinical trial study
Author: Seyyedi, Rafiean Kopaei, Miraj
Comment: Change-from-baseline scores (mean and SD of change) used for both arms because the paper reports no end-of-treatment means. MENQOL is oriented so a higher score = worse symptoms, so the recorded means must be sign-reversed before computing an SMD in which positive favours estrogen (after reversal, Premarin +4.83 vs lubricant +0.81, favouring estrogen). Three-arm trial: royal jelly arm excluded. Omnibus ANOVA p<0.001 across three groups; p=0.001 is the paper's own reported pairwise lubricant-vs-Premarin comparison. M_diff computed as group_2_mean − group_1_mean from explicitly reported means. Table 4 restates these values with means/SDs transposed and inconsistent group labels; Table 3 used.
Participant type: Married naturally postmenopausal women aged 50-65 years with symptoms of vaginal atrophy
Recruitment source: Gynecology and obstetrics clinics, Hajar Hospital, Shahrekord University of Medical Sciences, Iran
Outcome measurement: Mean ± SD change from baseline in MENQOL sexual function score at end of 3-month treatment
Outcome variable: Sexual function (MENQOL sexual-urinary problems domain, change from baseline; higher = worse)
additional_group_ns: Royal jelly vaginal cream 15% arm excluded per synthesis plan (not estrogen, not placebo): n=24 analysed, change -4.45 ± 2.93
effect_direction: favours estrogen (after sign reversal: vaginal conjugated estrogen improved substantially more than placebo lubricant, p=0.001)

Report_ID: MENQOL sexual function domain score, change from baseline to week 12 (higher = more bother / worse sexual function; sign must be reversed so higher = better)
Title: Effects of vaginal estradiol tablets and moisturizer on menopause-specific quality of life and mood in healthy postmenopausal women with vaginal symptoms: a randomized clinical trial
Author: Diem SJ, Guthrie KA, Mitchell CM, Reed SD, Larson JC, Ensrud KE, LaCroix AZ
Comment: Change-from-baseline scores used (end-of-treatment absolute means not reported); both arms use change scores. Per-arm SDs/SEs for the change are NOT reported — Table 2 gives 95% CIs only, so group SDs were left empty rather than derived. SE_diff was computed from the reported 95% CI of the mean difference as (0.1 - (-1.0))/3.92 = 0.281; note the printed CI (-1.0, 0.1) straddles 0 and appears inconsistent with the printed P=0.005 (possible typesetting error in the paper, same CI in abstract). Scale is bother-oriented (higher = worse), so means require sign reversal before SMD computation. Third arm (vaginal moisturizer) excluded per plan.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Vaginal estradiol 10 mcg tablet + placebo gel') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False); treatment SD derived from its reported mean CI; control SD derived from its reported mean CI
Participant type: Postmenopausal women aged 45-70 years with moderate-severe vulvovaginal symptoms
Recruitment source: Direct mailings and Facebook ads near Kaiser Permanente Washington Health Research Institute (Seattle) and University of Minnesota (Minneapolis)
Outcome measurement: Mean change from baseline (95% CI) per arm and between-arm adjusted mean difference from repeated-measures linear regression
Outcome variable: MENQOL sexual function domain score, change from baseline to week 12 (higher = more bother / worse sexual function; sign must be reversed so higher = better)
additional_group_ns: Excluded third arm (not matching the plan's estrogen or placebo definitions): vaginal moisturizer (Replens) + placebo tablet, n=98 at week 12 for the MENQOL sexual function domain (mean change -1.3, 95% CI -1.7, -0.9)
effect_direction: favours estrogen (vaginal estradiol change -2.3 vs placebo -1.8 on bother scale; after reversal favours estradiol, reported P=0.005)

Title: Ultralow 0.03 mg vaginal estriol in postmenopausal women who underwent surgical treatment for stress urinary incontinence: effects on quality of life and sexual function
Author: Caruso S, Cianci A, Sarpietro G, Matarazzo MG, Panella M, Cianci S
Comment: Control group received no treatment (no placebo); both arms underwent TOT surgery, so T2 values reflect surgery plus estriol in group A. Per-arm Ns are completers (36 vs 44). The earlier T1 time point (18.6 ± 1.3 vs 13.5 ± 1.2, P = 0.001) is the same outcome/comparison and was deduplicated in favour of the end-of-treatment T2 value.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Group A – 0.03 mg estriol vaginal ovule daily for 16 weeks + TOT') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Design Type: randomized controlled trial (no placebo; control = surgery alone/no treatment)
Participant type: postmenopausal women (47-73 y) with stress urinary incontinence scheduled for TOT placement
Recruitment source: Obstetrical Gynecological Unit, University of Catania, Italy
Outcome measurement: Mean ± SD FSFI total score at T2 (end of treatment)
effect_direction: favours estrogen (FSFI total 25.2 with vaginal estriol vs 17.2 no treatment, P=0.001)

Report_ID: FSFI total score change from baseline at week 12 (overall sexual function)
Title: Efficacy of Vaginal Estradiol or Vaginal Moisturizer vs Placebo for Treating Postmenopausal Vulvovaginal Symptoms: A Randomized Clinical Trial
Author: Mitchell CM, Reed SD, Diem S, Larson JC, Newton KM, Ensrud KE, LaCroix AZ, Caan B, Guthrie KA
Comment: Only mean CHANGE from baseline with 95% CIs is reported; no SDs of change are given for either arm (Table 1 reports baseline FSFI total SDs only: estradiol 5.9, moisturizer 6.5, placebo 6.6). Group SDs therefore left empty; per-arm 95% CIs recorded instead. SE_diff = (3.2 - (-1.2))/3.92 = 1.1224, derived from the reported 95% CI of the between-group difference. P = .64 is the model-based estradiol-vs-placebo P value for FSFI total across visits (printed on the week-4 row of Table 3 and repeated in the Abstract). Week-12 analysed Ns (64 estradiol, 70 placebo) are smaller than randomized Ns (102, 100) due to missing FSFI data.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Vaginal estradiol 10-µg tablet + placebo gel') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False); treatment SD derived from its reported mean CI; control SD derived from its reported mean CI
Design Type: randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, 3-arm parallel-group clinical trial
domain: menopause / women's health - genitourinary syndrome of menopause and sexual function
Study Environment: multicenter clinical trial (2 US academic/health-system sites)
Participant type: postmenopausal women aged 45-70 years with moderate-to-severe vulvovaginal symptoms (mean age 61 years, 81% sexually active)
Recruitment source: Direct mailings and Facebook advertisements near two clinical sites (Kaiser Permanente Washington Health Research Institute, Seattle; University of Minnesota, Minneapolis)
Outcome measurement: Mean change from baseline (week 12 minus baseline) with 95% CI per arm; between-group mean difference with 95% CI and P value from repeated-measures linear model adjusted for baseline value, visit, and site
Outcome variable: FSFI total score change from baseline at week 12 (overall sexual function)
additional_group_ns: Excluded third arm: vaginal moisturizer (Replens) + placebo tablet, n = 80 with week-12 FSFI total (n = 100 randomized) — excluded because the synthesis plan excludes vaginal moisturizer comparators
effect_direction: slightly favours estrogen but not significant (FSFI improvement 5.4 estradiol vs 4.5 placebo, difference 1.0, P=0.64)

Report_ID: Sexual function (WHQ Sexuality subscale) — mean percent change from baseline at 12 weeks
Title: Supplementation with DHEA: Effect on Muscle Size, Strength, Quality of Life, and Lipids
Author: Dayal, M.; Sammel, M.D.; Zhao, J.; Hummel, A.C.; Vandenbourne, K.; Barnhart, K.T.
Comment: Table 4 reports only the BASELINE mean ± SD and the mean PERCENT CHANGE from baseline; no end-of-treatment means/SDs and no SD of the change score are reported, so group_1_sd/group_2_sd are intentionally left empty and no SMD can be validly computed from the reported data. The SDs shown in Table 4 (ET 1.53; placebo 2.12) belong to the BASELINE scores (ET baseline 4.33, placebo baseline 5.00), not to the percent-change values recorded here. Group means recorded are percent changes (ET -14%, placebo +18%). Placebo n = 5 for QOL/well-being measures (vs n = 6 randomized). No between-group test statistic or p value is reported for the sexuality subscale; the text states only that no significant differences were noted. Scale orientation: the paper treats a higher WHQ sexuality score as better ("Feelings of sexuality were improved in the DHEA-ET and placebo groups", which had positive change), so no sign reversal was applied.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Conjugated equine estrogen (CEE) 0.625 mg daily (ET)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False); proportions out of valid range or equal — cannot compute OR
Recruitment source: Advertisements in local media; University of Pennsylvania Medical Center (tertiary care center)
Outcome measurement: Mean baseline score (± SD) and mean percent change from baseline over 12 weeks, by treatment group (Table 4)
Outcome variable: Sexual function (WHQ Sexuality subscale) — mean percent change from baseline at 12 weeks
additional_group_ns: Excluded arms (not matching the plan's treatment/control definitions): DHEA 50 mg alone n = 12 (sexuality baseline 5.67 ± 1.66, -11% change); DHEA 50 mg + CEE 0.625 mg (DHEA-ET) n = 9 (sexuality baseline 5.43 ± 1.72, +31% change)
effect_direction: favours placebo (CEE -14% vs placebo +18% change in WHQ sexuality; no significant difference reported)

Report_ID: McCoy Sex Scale total score at 3 months (higher = better sexual function)
Title: Quality of life of postmenopausal women on a regimen of transdermal estradiol therapy: A double-blind placebo-controlled study
Author: Wiklund, Karlberg, Mattsson
Comment: M_diff computed as group_2_mean - group_1_mean (41.5 - 46.0 = -4.5) where group_1 is the estradiol arm as listed first in the paper's own table; group_1_is_control=False indicates arm identity. End-of-treatment (3-month) means used, as required by the plan. The p value is the paper's between-group significance for the mean difference.; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Transdermal estradiol therapy 50 µg/24 h') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
domain: menopause / hormone replacement therapy / sexual function
Participant type: Postmenopausal women aged 45-65 years with climacteric symptoms, natural menopause
Recruitment source: 15 gynecology centres; gynecologist visits and local newspaper advertisement
Outcome measurement: Self-administered questionnaire; mean and SD per arm at 3 months

Report_ID: Greene Climacteric Scale sexual dysfunction subscale score (mean change from baseline at week 13)
Title: Efficacy and Tolerability of a Novel Estradiol Vaginal Ring for Relief of Menopausal Symptoms
Author: Speroff L, for the United States VR Investigator Group
Comment: No SD, SE or CI is reported for any Greene Climacteric Scale subscale score, so a standardised mean difference cannot be computed from the paper's own data; only mean change values and the threshold P<.002 are given. Values are mean CHANGE from baseline (LOCF), not end-of-treatment values. The scale is bother/severity-oriented (higher = worse), so means must be sign-reversed before computing an SMD favouring estrogen. Baseline imbalance: placebo had a higher (worse) baseline subscale score (1.59) than the 50 µg (1.14) and 100 µg (1.17) arms, as acknowledged in the text. Per the synthesis plan the two estradiol dose arms should be combined, but pooled means/SDs cannot be computed because no SDs are reported; the 100 µg arm is therefore recorded verbatim in additional_group_ns. P-value recorded as the reported threshold (P<.002), not an exact value.; ANOVA: missing F-value or group sizes; N-INCONSISTENCY: n_control(105) + n_treatment(111) = 216 ≠ n_total(325) — verify per-group Ns
Participant type: healthy postmenopausal women with moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms
Recruitment source: 35 clinical sites in the United States
Outcome measurement: Mean change from baseline in Greene Climacteric Scale sexual dysfunction subscale at week 13 (higher score = more/worse symptoms; a more negative change = improvement)
Outcome variable: Greene Climacteric Scale sexual dysfunction subscale score (mean change from baseline at week 13)
additional_group_ns: Third arm not entered into group_1/group_2 fields: Estradiol vaginal ring 100 µg/day, n=109 (mITT), mean change at week 13 = -0.69, P<.002 vs placebo. Baseline sexual dysfunction subscale scores: 1.14 (50 µg), 1.17 (100 µg), 1.59 (placebo).
effect_direction: favours estrogen (estradiol ring change -0.72 [50 µg] and -0.69 [100 µg] vs placebo -0.56 on severity scale, P<.002)

Title: Effects of vaginal administration of conjugated estrogens tablet on sexual function in postmenopausal women with sexual dysfunction: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial
Author: Bumphenkiatikul et al.
Comment: Table 3 week-0 and week-12 columns are interleaved in the extracted text; values assigned as estrogens week 0 = 20.31 ± 4.93, estrogens week 12 = 25.14 ± 4.74, placebo week 0 = 22.27 ± 5.03, placebo week 12 = 24.32 ± 4.83 per the pre-identified effect. Ns are randomized/ITT (multiple imputation); 58 participants completed. Abstract reverses the arm Ns (estrogens n=33, placebo n=34).; group_1/group_2 fields swapped: the extractor itself stated group_1_label ('Vaginal conjugated estrogens tablet (Estromon 0.625 mg)') is the intervention arm (group_1_is_control=False)
Participant type: postmenopausal Thai women aged 45–70 years with female sexual dysfunction (FSFI ≤ 26.55) and symptomatic vaginal atrophy (pH > 5)
Recruitment source: General Gynecologic Clinic, Climacteric and Gender Health Clinic, King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital
Outcome measurement: Mean ± SD FSFI total score at week 12 per arm; between-arm comparison by ANCOVA with baseline as covariate
effect_direction: slightly favours estrogen but not significant (FSFI total 25.14 vs placebo 24.32 at week 12, p=0.182)
